keyword: how to get rid of ants in kitchen
metaTitle: How to Get Rid of Ants in the Kitchen: Use Bait
metaDescription: Follow the trail, wipe it with soapy water, seal food and gaps, then bait beside the trail and off the counter. Plus what not to spray near food.
h1: How to Get Rid of Ants in the Kitchen: Find the Trail, Clean, Seal, Then Bait
dek: A kitchen-specific plan built from university extension and EPA guidance: where the ants are getting in, how to clear the trail, where bait can go near food, and what should never be sprayed where you cook.
excerpt: Kitchen ants come for food and water and nest out of sight. How to find the entry point, clean the trail, place bait off food surfaces and avoid spraying where you cook.

quickAnswer.lead: **To get rid of ants in the kitchen, follow the trail to where it comes in, wipe it away with soapy water, put food and water out of reach, seal the gap, and bait only if the ants keep coming.** The [University of California](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/ants/) says indoor sprays are not necessary when ants can be washed away and kept out. Bait goes beside the trail, never on a food-preparation surface.
bullets: The ants on the counter are a small portion of the colony; the University of Kentucky says thousands more, including the egg-laying queens, stay hidden in the nest.
Soapy water removes the scent trail that leads other workers to the food, according to the University of California.
Indoor nests are out of sight: behind cabinets and appliances, in door and window frames, and in wall voids near heat and moisture.
The EPA says not to let a pesticide get on any surface used for food preparation and never to put insect bait where small children or pets can reach it.
The University of California says bait can take 5 to 10 days to thin the trail and several weeks or more to finish the job.
Texas A&M says spraying an ant trail kills only a few foragers and can sometimes split a colony into two or more.

body.text: What is the fastest way to get rid of ants in the kitchen?

Wash them away and close the route they used, then bait only if they come back. The [University of California's Pest Notes on ants](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/ants/) says that when ants can be thoroughly washed away and excluded from an area, indoor insecticide sprays are not necessary, and that vacuuming a trail, or sponging or mopping it with soapy water, may be as effective as an insecticide spray at temporarily removing foraging ants. The order matters, because the trail is your only map to the entry point:

items: **Follow the trail before you touch it.** Trace the line of ants back from the food to the crack, pipe opening or frame it comes out of.
**Wipe up the ants and the trail with soapy water.** Clean most thoroughly at the entry point.
**Take away what they came for.** Close up the food, wipe up grease and spills, and dry up any water.
**Seal the opening.** Caulk the crack or gap the trail came through.
**Bait if they keep coming, or if you cannot find the way in.** Set a slow-acting bait beside the trail and off every food surface, then stop cleaning around it.

body.text: A spray is missing from that list for a reason. The [University of Kentucky's guide to ant control for householders](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef619) explains that the ants seen on exposed surfaces are only a small portion of the colony, and that thousands more, including one or more egg-laying queens, are typically hidden in a nest. Killing the foragers leaves the colony in place. The sections below take each step in a kitchen setting; for bedrooms, bathrooms and basements, see [the whole-house plan for ants indoors](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-in-the-house).
Why do ants come into the kitchen?

Because the kitchen puts food and water in the same room. [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's bulletin on household ants](https://extensionentomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Ants_household_B6183.pdf) says ants enter a home in search of food, water or a good nesting site, and the University of California adds warmth, shelter and refuge from hot, dry weather or flooding. The Texas bulletin also explains why a few ants turn into a line: foraging workers of some species lay chemical (pheromone) trails that lead other ants to food and water.

What they want depends on the species. The University of California lists sweets as the main food of Argentine ants and odorous house ants, fats, proteins and sweets for pharaoh ants, and greasy and fatty foods for thief ants. Notice whether your ants are at the sugar bowl or at the grease beside the stove, because that is a clue to which bait they will take later. Related guides cover [what each household ant species eats](/blog/what-do-ants-eat), [the small sweet-feeding ants most people call sugar ants](/blog/sugar-ants) and [how to tell very small kitchen ants apart](/blog/tiny-ants), and [the complete reference to ants in US homes](/learn/ants) explains how a colony is organized.
Where do kitchen ants nest, and how do they get in?

Many of them do not nest in the kitchen at all: they live outdoors and walk in along pipes, wires and the edges of the building. Texas A&M says some species commonly nest indoors while others nest outside and enter a home just to look for food, and it lists wires, hoses and plumbing systems among the routes ants use as highways. The University of California notes that ants usually nest in soil, often next to buildings. The species that do move indoors pick hidden spots close to warmth and water, and a kitchen has several.

head: Where to look
What the sources say
rows: The cabinet under the sink, and along pipes
The University of California says to inspect under sinks, in cupboards, and along pipes and electrical wires, and that leaky faucets attract thirsty ants.
Behind cabinets and appliances

The University of Kentucky lists the spaces behind walls, cabinets and appliances as indoor nest sites, and says odorous house ants nest in wall cavities, appliances and potted plants, especially near sources of moisture.
Door and window frames
The University of Kentucky and Iowa State University both name door and window frames as places colonies hide.
Wall voids near heat and water

The University of California says that in temperate climates pharaoh ants nest in warm, moist locations such as inside wall voids, under flooring, or near hot water pipes or heating systems, and that odorous house ants nest indoors in wall voids or around water pipes or heaters.
Damp or rotting wood
Texas A&M says carpenter ants may prefer moist or decaying wood.

body.text: None of these sources singles out the dishwasher by name, but it matches their description on every count: an appliance set against a wall, with a water supply, a drain and heat. Check the gap around it and the point where its water line and drain hose pass through the side of the sink cabinet.

body.text: How do you follow the trail to the entry point?

Watch the ants for a few minutes before you clean anything. The University of California advises following a trail to where the ants are entering the building, and to the nest if possible, and looking indoors and outdoors for holes or cracks in foundations and walls. Texas A&M suggests observing both during the day and after dark, since some ants are more active at night, and noting which foods they go to and where most of them appear.

If the trail is too thin to follow, the Texas bulletin describes a lure: put sugar water, peanut butter, mint apple jelly or bacon grease on a small square of aluminum foil or in a bottle cap, then watch where the ants carry it. You may still not find the nest. Texas A&M notes that most indoor nests cannot be seen because they are in wall voids or underneath slabs. Knowing the opening the ants use is enough for the steps that follow.

Two findings change the plan. Winged ants swarming inside the home mean the colony is likely somewhere indoors, according to Texas A&M; a separate guide explains [what an indoor swarm of flying ants means](/blog/flying-ants). And ants 1/4 to 1/2 inch long, the size the bulletin gives for carpenter ant workers, point toward a nest in wood, where the job is [finding and treating the carpenter ant nest](/blog/carpenter-ants-canada) and not baiting a countertop trail.
How do you clean an ant trail off kitchen surfaces?

Use a sponge and soapy water. The University of California says soapy water removes the ants' scent trail, especially when the entry point is cleaned thoroughly, and the [National Pesticide Information Center's page on ants](https://npic.orst.edu/pest/ant.html) gives the same advice: wipe up trails with soapy water to remove the pheromone. Both also suggest a vacuum for the ants themselves, and the center adds that the vacuum bag should be thrown out right away.

Treat this as a reset, not a cure. The University of Kentucky describes wiping away the invisible odor trail with a kitchen cleanser or mild detergent as temporary relief. If the food is still out and the gap is still open, scouts will find their way back. Vinegar is the other cleaner people reach for, and a separate page looks at [what vinegar does and does not do to ants and their trails](/blog/does-vinegar-kill-ants).

body.title: Baiting? Clean first, then stop
body.text: The University of Kentucky says not to disturb foraging trails while a bait is out, and not to use cleaning agents around the bait, because they may keep ants from approaching and eating it.
How should you store food so ants lose interest?

Put the foods ants want in containers that close, and clean the outside of those containers as well. The University of California names sugar, syrup, honey and pet food as items to keep in closed containers that have been washed to remove residue from their outer surfaces. The [EPA's Citizen's Guide to Pest Control and Pesticide Safety](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-08/documents/citizens_guide_to_pest_control_and_pesticide_safety.pdf) recommends sealed glass or plastic containers and a kitchen kept free of cooking grease and oil. The rest of the routine:

items: **Spills and crumbs.** The University of California says to clean up grease and spills thoroughly and, to help a bait work, to clear food particles and sweet residues out of the cracks around sinks and pantries.
**Sticky empties.** Rinse out empty soft drink containers or take them out of the building, the same university advises.

**Garbage.** The University of California says to remove garbage daily and change liners frequently, the EPA calls for tightly covered cans, and the National Pesticide Information Center adds regularly emptying and washing garbage cans and recycling bins.
**Pet food.** The EPA guide says not to leave food in pet bowls on the counter or floor for long periods.
**Water.** Texas A&M says to repair dripping faucets and other plumbing leaks, and the EPA says not to leave water in trays under houseplants or under the refrigerator.

body.text: A tidy counter is not the whole answer, because ants also come for water and shelter. The EPA guide gives its food and water advice for household pests in general, not only ants, and [the complete reference to cockroaches in US homes](/learn/cockroaches) covers another pest it applies to.
Where should ant bait go in a kitchen?

Beside the trail, in a spot that food, children and pets never touch. Three rules from the sources set the limits. The University of Kentucky and [Iowa State University Extension](https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/ant-baits-small-household-ants) both say to place bait next to wherever ants are seen; Kentucky adds preferably beside a trail, and Iowa State's examples are in corners and along walls. The EPA guide says not to let pesticides get on any surface used for food preparation, and never to put insect bait where small children or pets can reach it. And the University of California describes gel baits as applied in the small cracks and crevices where ants are entering.

Bait is a pesticide, so the cautious reading of the EPA rule is to keep it off the countertop, the cutting board and the pantry shelf, even when the trail runs straight across them. Kentucky's fact sheet does count countertops among the surfaces masking tape can protect under a dab of gel bait, so check what the product label allows. In most kitchens, the placements that satisfy all three rules are these:

items: **The back of the cabinet under the sink,** beside the pipe openings the ants are using, if the door is latched or no small children or pets live in the home.
**The gap beside or behind the stove, refrigerator or dishwasher,** at the point where the trail disappears.
**The floor-and-wall corner or baseboard crack** the trail comes out of, if it is out of reach of children and pets.
**A crack in a window or door frame** the ants are entering through, as long as the bait cannot drip or be knocked onto a food surface.

body.text: If the trail crosses a counter, follow it to where it leaves the counter and bait there. For gel or liquid bait, Kentucky and Iowa State suggest putting small dabs on the non-sticky side of a piece of masking tape or on wax paper, which Kentucky says protects the surface underneath. A related guide explains [what a bait station does that a sticky trap cannot](/blog/best-ant-traps-canada).

body.text: Should you bait indoors at all?

The sources differ here. Kentucky and Iowa State tell readers to bait indoors, next to wherever the ants are seen. The University of California says to use baits primarily outdoors, and indoors only when the infestation is serious and you cannot find the spot where ants are entering, because bait inside could attract ants indoors while outdoor bait draws them out of the building. It is writing for California, where it names the Argentine ant, listed in its table as nesting outdoors in shallow mounds, as the most common ant in and around the house.

For a kitchen, a reasonable reading is this. If you found the entry point, clean, seal and, where the label allows outdoor use, bait outside near the trail. If you could not find it, or the ants seem to be coming from inside the walls, bait indoors.
How do you get the bait to work?

items: **Match the food.** The University of Kentucky notes that ants are finicky and may change their preferences through the year, and the University of California says that if ants are not taking a bait you should reposition it or try a different product. A companion page explains [how borax baits work and why a weak mix beats a strong one](/blog/borax-for-ants).

**Read the active ingredient.** The University of California lists boric acid or borate, fipronil, avermectin and hydramethylnon as ingredients found in ant baits. All are slow-acting on purpose, so workers live long enough to share the bait in the nest.
**Clear competing food.** Texas A&M says bait is more effective once other food sources such as spilled food and grease are removed.

**No sprays nearby.** The University of California says not to use any insecticide spray while baiting, Texas A&M explains that sprays keep foraging workers from reaching the bait, and Iowa State says not to place bait directly on a surface previously treated with insecticide.
**Expect more ants at first.** Kentucky says an early increase in ants around the bait shows they are feeding and carrying it back to the nest, and tells readers not to spray them.

**Give it time.** Kentucky says activity usually subsides in a few days. The University of California says it can take 5 to 10 days to see fewer ants and several weeks or more for control to be complete, and Texas A&M says some colonies take 3 to 4 weeks or more.

**Keep it fresh.** The University of California notes that some bait products dry up rapidly and must be replaced frequently, and Kentucky says to keep placing additional baits wherever ants are seen.
**Clean up at the end.** Iowa State says to discard uneaten bait carefully and wash any remaining residue off surfaces with soap and water.

body.title: The label is the law
body.text: Every ant bait and spray is a pesticide. Use it only where and how the label directs, and keep it off food, dishes and food-preparation surfaces. If someone swallows bait, follow the first aid directions on the label and call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222; for a pet, call your veterinarian.
What should you not spray where food is prepared?

Do not spray countertops, tables, cutting boards or any other surface used for food preparation, and do not spray inside cabinets that still hold food or dishes. The EPA guide is specific: use pesticides indoors only when absolutely necessary and in very limited amounts, apply most surface sprays only to limited areas such as cracks, and do not treat entire floors, walls or ceilings. Before treating kitchen cabinets, it says to remove food, pots and pans, and dishes, to wait until shelves dry before refilling them, and to wash any surface that may have pesticide residue before food goes on it. The guide is dated March 2005, so where a current product label is stricter, the label governs.

head: Avoid
What the sources say
rows: Spraying the trail on the counter

Texas A&M says insecticide sprayed on ant trails kills only a few foraging workers, does not eliminate colonies, and can sometimes make the problem worse by causing a colony to split into two or more. It also puts pesticide on a food surface.
Foggers in or under cabinets and counters

The EPA says total release foggers should not be used in small, enclosed places such as closets and cabinets or under tables and counters, and must be kept away from ignition sources such as ovens and stoves.
Kitchen measuring cups or spoons for a pesticide
The EPA says never to use the same measuring cups or spoons that you use in the kitchen.
Keeping ant products in a food cabinet
The EPA says never to store pesticides in cabinets with or near food.

body.text: A spray has one narrow place in this plan. Texas A&M says repellent pyrethroid sprays should not be used while baits are set out, but can be used after a baiting program around cracks, plumbing openings and other places ants might enter, to keep them from reinfesting a home. If you do that, choose a product labeled for that use indoors, follow the label, and keep it to the cracks. The National Pesticide Information Center's advice is to try a lower toxicity product first. A related page sets out [why baiting outperforms spraying against an ant colony](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-canada).
How do you keep ants from coming back to the kitchen?

Seal the openings and take away the moisture. The University of California recommends eliminating cracks and crevices wherever possible indoors, especially in kitchens and other food-preparation and storage areas, and caulking the cracks that provide entry from outside. Work through the routes the trail showed you:

items: **Pipe and wire openings.** The University of Kentucky says to seal the openings where utility pipes and wires enter the building.
**Doors and windows.** Kentucky says to seal around door thresholds and windows, and Texas A&M says to replace worn weatherstripping.
**Leaks and damp wood.** Texas A&M says to replace wet or rotten wood, and the National Pesticide Information Center likewise advises fixing leaky pipes and replacing moisture-damaged wood.

**Plants touching the house.** Kentucky advises trimming back shrubs and vegetation that touch the building, and Texas A&M says to trim tree limbs away from the roof and house because ants may use them as bridges.

**Things you carry in.** Texas A&M says to check firewood and potted plants for ants before bringing them indoors. If a houseplant already holds a nest, the University of California's method is to take the pot out of the building and stand it for 20 minutes or more in a solution of insecticidal soap and water.

body.text: If you baited indoors, it makes sense to seal the opening the ants themselves are using last. Iowa State points out that a bait works only if the ants eat it and also return to the colony, and closing their route while they are still feeding would cut them off from it.
When should you call a professional about kitchen ants?

Call one when the trail keeps returning after several weeks of correct baiting, when the nest is inside a wall or in wood, or when the ants are carpenter ants. Texas A&M says plainly that ant control can be difficult and that if you are not successful you should call a commercial pest control operator. It adds that reaching a colony sometimes means drilling into wood or wall voids, which calls for a professional's skill and equipment, and that a professional's help may be important with species such as carpenter ants that keep satellite colonies apart from the main nest. The University of Kentucky notes that pest control firms have more experience with ants and a broader range of insecticides and application equipment than the public.

Pharaoh ants are worth recognizing before you treat, because Texas A&M lists them as a species that usually nests indoors. The bulletin describes them as about 1/12 to 1/16 inch long and light tan to reddish, nesting near sources of heat and moisture, with trails that can reach 150 feet. Their colonies multiply by budding, in which a large part of a colony moves to a new nesting site. When a pharaoh ant nest cannot be located, the bulletin's recommendation is a bait.

When you hire a company, the University of California suggests asking it to use baits and spot treatments in place of perimeter treatments or monthly sprays. For budgeting, see [what professional pest control typically costs](/blog/how-much-is-pest-control).

howTo.name: How to get rid of ants in the kitchen

steps.name: Follow the trail
steps.text: Before cleaning anything, trace the line of ants back from the food to the crack, pipe opening, appliance gap or window frame where it enters the kitchen.

steps.name: Wipe up the ants and the trail
steps.text: Sponge the ants and their path with soapy water, cleaning most thoroughly at the entry point, to remove the scent trail other workers follow.

steps.name: Remove food and water
steps.text: Move sugar, syrup, honey and pet food into closed containers, wipe up grease and spills, take out the garbage, and fix dripping faucets or leaks under the sink.

steps.name: Seal the entry point
steps.text: Caulk the crack or gap the trail came through, and replace worn weatherstripping if the ants were entering at a door or window.

steps.name: Place bait beside the trail
steps.text: If ants keep coming or the entry cannot be found, set a slow-acting ant bait next to the trail, off every food-preparation surface and out of reach of children and pets.

steps.name: Leave the bait and the ants alone
steps.text: Do not spray insecticide or use cleaners near the bait, and tolerate the extra ants that gather there during the first days of feeding.

steps.name: Refresh or switch the bait
steps.text: Replace bait that is empty or dried out, and move it or try a different product if the ants ignore it, for as long as ants are still arriving.

steps.name: Clean up and close the gap
steps.text: When activity stops, discard leftover bait as the label directs, wash any residue off surfaces with soap and water, and seal the opening the ants were using.

faqs.question: Why do ants keep coming back to a clean kitchen?
faqs.answer: Because food is only one of the things they come for. The University of California says ants enter buildings seeking food and water, warmth and shelter, or refuge from hot, dry weather or flooding, and that leaky faucets attract thirsty ants. Texas A&M adds that colonies may move indoors when the weather is abnormally hot and dry or very wet. A spotless counter does nothing about a dripping pipe under the sink, a nest in the wall, or an open crack at a window frame. Fix the moisture, seal the opening the trail uses, and bait if the ants are still arriving.

faqs.question: Can you put ant bait on a kitchen counter?
faqs.answer: It is better not to. Ant bait is a pesticide, and the EPA's Citizen's Guide to Pest Control and Pesticide Safety says not to let pesticides get on any surface used for food preparation and never to put insect bait where small children or pets can reach it. If the trail crosses the counter, follow it to the point where it leaves, such as a crack at the backsplash, a window frame or the gap beside the stove, and bait there. When the ants are gone, Iowa State University Extension advises discarding leftover bait carefully and washing any residue off surfaces with soap and water.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get rid of ants in the kitchen?
faqs.answer: Wiping up a trail with soapy water clears the ants in sight right away, but the relief is temporary while the colony is still active. With bait, the University of Kentucky says ant activity usually subsides in a few days. The University of California says it can take 5 to 10 days to see fewer ants and several weeks or more for control to be complete, and Texas A&M says some colonies take 3 to 4 weeks or more. Keep fresh bait available for that whole period, and do not spray or clean around it.

faqs.question: Do ants in the kitchen mean there is a nest inside the house?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension says some species commonly nest indoors while others nest outside and come in only to look for food, and the University of California notes that ants usually nest in soil, often next to buildings. Following the trail helps you tell which you have: a trail that leads to a crack in an outside wall, a window frame or a pipe opening may come from a nest outdoors. Winged ants swarming inside the home are a different sign. Texas A&M says that when this happens, the colony is likely located somewhere inside.

faqs.question: Should you kill the ants you see on the counter?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether bait is out. If you are not baiting, yes: the University of California advises cleaning up invading ants with a sponge and soapy water as soon as they come in, which also removes their scent trail. If you have set bait, leave the ants walking to and from it alone. The University of Kentucky warns against spraying ants that gather at a bait or disturbing their foraging trails, and Iowa State University Extension explains that a bait only works when ants eat it and return to the colony.

faqs.question: What can you use for kitchen ants if you have small children or pets?
faqs.answer: Start with the steps that involve no pesticide. The University of California says indoor sprays are not necessary when ants can be thoroughly washed away and excluded from an area, which in practice means soapy water and a sealed entry point, and closed food containers and repaired leaks remove what they came for. If bait is needed, the same university describes prepackaged bait stations as easy to use and quite safe if kept away from children and pets, and the EPA says never to put insect bait where small children or pets can reach it. The National Pesticide Information Center suggests trying a lower toxicity product first and answers pesticide questions at 1-800-858-7378.
